technique.how: Divide the heart rate (beats/min) by the systolic blood pressure (mmHg) from the first set of triage vital signs; normal is roughly 0.5-0.7. Record the threshold used (>0.9 or >=1.0) and recalculate with each new set of vitals to follow the trend.
technique.prerequisites: Accurate HR and SBP; note beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, pacemakers and baseline hypertension.

interpretation.positive_finding: SI >0.9 in trauma has specificity ~94% for hemorrhage needing hemostasis (LR+ ~8.5 computed) and SI >=1.0 in suspected infection is the most specific vital-sign predictor of hyperlactatemia (spec 0.81); an elevated SI flags occult shock when HR and SBP each look acceptable.
interpretation.negative_finding: A normal SI does not exclude bleeding or sepsis (sensitivity 55% for hemorrhage at >0.9; 48% for lactate >=4 at >=1.0); lowering the threshold to 0.7-0.8 improves sensitivity at the cost of specificity.
interpretation.pitfalls: Beta-blockade, pacing, hypertension and age blunt the index; pain, anxiety, fever, and anemia raise it without shock. A single value is less informative than the trend.
interpretation.changes_what: Elevated SI: escalate to resuscitation, early lactate, source/bleeding search and transfusion readiness; normal SI: do not de-escalate on this alone.

estimates.target_condition: Hemorrhage requiring hemostasis intervention after trauma — SI >0.9 (initial hospital vitals)
estimates.population: 4277 adult (>16 y) trauma patients at a single trauma centre over 11 years; traumatic brain injury and transfers excluded; retrospective
estimates.reference_standard: Bleeding requiring intervention for hemostasis (study definition; the Koch 2019 review summarises it as >=2 units PRBC in 24 h)
estimates.quote: using the standard SI cutoff of >0.9 as the threshold for bleeding, the sensitivity is 54.5%, with a specificity of 93.6%
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.545/(1-0.936) = 8.52; LR- = (1-0.545)/0.936 = 0.49; from reported sensitivity 54.5% and specificity 93.6%

estimates.target_condition: Hemorrhage requiring hemostasis intervention after trauma — SI >=0.8 (lowered threshold)
estimates.population: 4277 adult (>16 y) trauma patients at a single trauma centre over 11 years; traumatic brain injury and transfers excluded; retrospective
estimates.reference_standard: Bleeding requiring intervention for hemostasis (study definition; the Koch 2019 review summarises it as >=2 units PRBC in 24 h)
estimates.quote: Lowering the SI to ≥0.8 increases the sensitivity to 76.1%, with a specificity of 87.4%
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.761/(1-0.874) = 6.04; LR- = (1-0.761)/0.874 = 0.27; from reported sensitivity 76.1% and specificity 87.4%

estimates.target_condition: Hyperlactatemia (lactate >=4.0 mmol/L) in ED patients with suspected infection — SI >=1.0 at triage
estimates.population: 2524 adult ED patients with suspected infection screened for severe sepsis; retrospective; hyperlactatemia in 290 (11.5%)
estimates.reference_standard: Initial serum lactate >=4.0 mmol/L (hyperlactatemia as surrogate for severe sepsis)
estimates.location: Full text (PMC), Table 3 'Performance of predictors for hyperlactatemia', column SI ≥ 1.0
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.48/(1-0.81) = 2.53; LR- = (1-0.48)/0.81 = 0.64; from Table 3 sensitivity 0.48, specificity 0.81 (SI ≥1.0 column)

estimates.target_condition: Hyperlactatemia (lactate >=4.0 mmol/L) in ED patients with suspected infection — SI >=0.7 at triage
estimates.population: 2524 adult ED patients with suspected infection screened for severe sepsis; retrospective; hyperlactatemia in 290 (11.5%)
estimates.reference_standard: Initial serum lactate >=4.0 mmol/L (hyperlactatemia as surrogate for severe sepsis)
estimates.location: Full text (PMC), Table 3 'Performance of predictors for hyperlactatemia', column SI ≥ 0.7
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.83/(1-0.42) = 1.43; LR- = (1-0.83)/0.42 = 0.40; from Table 3 sensitivity 0.83, specificity 0.42 (SI ≥0.7 column)

estimates.target_condition: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy (hemoperitoneum) — SI (HR/SBP) >0.7 at presentation; case-control design
estimates.population: 52 ED patients with ectopic pregnancy (25 ruptured, 27 unruptured); retrospective case-control
estimates.quote: sensitivity for heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and heart rate/systolic blood pressure was 28%, 36%, and 72% respectively; the specificity was 96%, 96%, and 67%

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on SI in patients on beta-blockers or with pacemakers, in pregnancy beyond the first trimester, or in children (use age-adjusted SIPA).
safety_scope.escalation_warning: SI >=1.0 with a bleeding source, suspected AAA, PE or infection indicates shock and warrants immediate resuscitation, senior review and ICU-level care.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Derived from measured vitals; variation comes from measurement timing and technique rather than observer judgement.

extraction_notes: Primary cohorts were traced through the Koch 2019 narrative review (source 3, used as an index only; tagged consensus for lack of a closer kind). DeMuro 2013 (trauma) and Berger 2013 (suspected infection) give sensitivity/specificity for the title thresholds; LRs are computed from those pairs and flagged computed=true. The Berger quote is the verbatim Table 3 row (columns in order: SI ≥1.0, SIRS, SI ≥0.7, SIRS without WBC). Birkhahn 2003 is a case-control study, so no prevalence is entered; ectopic pregnancy is not in vocab.json and is included only because ruptured ectopic is a hemorrhagic-shock cause in women with abdominal pain/syncope. Prognostic data not entered as diagnostic: Berger Table 4 28-day mortality (SI ≥1.0 sensitivity 0.37, specificity 0.8); Mutschler 2013 (n=21,853) mortality rose from 10.9% (SI <0.6) to 39.8% (SI ≥1.4) and '31% in group III and 57% in group IV required ≥10 blood units' (Abstract, Results) — PROGNOSTIC strata, not accuracy. DeMuro abstract: geriatric subgroup 'SI is more specific in the older patients' without numbers.
